references.text: The Israelites complain to Moses again, saying they would rather have died in Egypt—a recurring theme of discontent in the wilderness.
The people grumble against Moses and ask why he brought them out of Egypt, the same accusatory question as in 14:11.
The Israelites complain and long to return to Egypt, a pattern that began at the Red Sea.
The people wish to die in the wilderness rather than enter the Promised Land, accusing Moses of bringing them out of Egypt.
The Israelites ask why Moses brought them into the wilderness to die there, the same complaint as at the Red Sea.
The people speak against God and Moses, complaining that they were brought out of Egypt only to die in the wilderness.
The psalm describes how the fathers at the Red Sea did not understand God's wonders and were rebellious.
Stephen describes how the Israelites turned back in their hearts to Egypt and rejected Moses.
Direct parallel: The wish to die in Egypt or the wilderness as an expression of distrust in God's guidance.
Recurring pattern: The accusation of being brought out only to die in the wilderness is repeated at Kadesh.
Rhetorical parallel: The accusation of being led into danger and death in the wilderness is also used in power struggles.
Identical theological accusation: The wilderness is seen as a place of death rather than life.
